A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bias-diversity analysis and MAMBR approach despite v2's retitling and expanded theoretical scope. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation, summarization, and captioning experiments, including correlation analyses, MAMBR comparisons, and appendix sensitivity studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports MAMBR runtime and GPU-memory measurements in Appendix E.1.

M1.justification: MAMBR retains the same averaging over pseudo-references and metric models trained with different seeds: v1 Equation 11 matches v2 Equation 15. Pseudo-bias remains the same gold-reference approximation; the expanded theory does not introduce a different decoding procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WMT19 En-De and En-Ru, SAMSum, XSum, MSCOCO, and NoCaps, with the same metric-training datasets and first-1000-example studies. The broader discussion of inference methods introduces no additional evaluated tasks or populations.

E2.justification: The evaluated sampling strategies and MAMBR model-count comparisons are retained. The epsilon-sampling and beam-decoding comparisons in v1 Tables 2–3 move to v2 Tables 4–5; newly discussed methods such as Daheim et al. are not added as experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 replaces correlations pooled after dataset-wise z-score normalization with averages obtained through Fisher z-transformation. Appendix E.1 also introduces runtime and memory measurement on one RTX A6000 across existing MAMBR configurations. The underlying task-performance evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix E.1 adds an analysis of computational costs across model and pseudo-reference counts. Existing cross-metric checks, hypothesis-sampling analyses, and subset studies are retained. The new inference-scaling discussion reinterprets Figure 2 rather than adding an independent scaling experiment.

E5.justification: v2 adds significance annotations for dataset-level correlations in Figures 1 and 3, specifying Student's t-test and p < 0.05; aggregate averages are excluded. v1 lacks this significance reporting. The eight metric models trained with varying seeds were already documented in v1.

E6.justification: All 720 scores in the six matched MAMBR tables and the individual-dataset correlation coefficients are unchanged. v2 adds runtime and memory results in Tables 2–3 and replaces pooled correlation summaries with Fisher-z averages: Figure 1's overall-diversity Spearman summary changes from 0.31 to 0.46 under this different aggregation procedure.

T1.justification: Beyond reorganizing the existing decomposition and ensemble results, v2 introduces a bias-variance-covariance reformulation and information-theoretic error bounds, monotonicity, and submodularity claims in Theorems 3–8. Appendix A adds corresponding proof discussions, several referring to proofs in other works rather than supplying derivations.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on explaining MBR through bias-diversity decomposition, pseudo-bias, and MAMBR. v2's title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion additionally claim that diversity explains inference scaling laws beyond MBR, substantially broadening the central scientific claim.

C2.justification: New Sections 3.4.5–3.4.7 and 5.4 interpret hypothesis diversity, other decoding methods, conditional independence, and sample interactions through the scaling framework. The previous limitation concerning hypothesis diversity is narrowed to the bias-diversity decomposition, because v2 claims its information-theoretic analysis addresses that limitation.

D1.justification: v2 adds resource measurements and their single-GPU measurement context in Appendix E.1, and model-license information in Appendix G. The abstract changes the code-release statement from planned availability to reported availability. The principal hardware identities and training settings were already disclosed in v1.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around information-theoretic ensembles, self-consistency, and inference scaling, citing works including Brown (2009), Zhou and Li (2010), and Snell et al. (2025). It also replaces v1's suggestion that combining metrics had not been applied to MBR with discussion of Kovacs et al. (2024), and distinguishes MAMBR from Daheim et al. (2025).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten around inference scaling. The theoretical exposition and appendix organization change, MAMBR discussion is redistributed, limitations move into the main text, and the reproducibility statement moves to Appendix G.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout, with extensive repositioning and resizing of displays. Figures 1–2 share a page, correlation heatmaps gain significance annotations, two computational-cost tables are added, and the epsilon/beam result tables move into the appendix.

improvement.justification: Significance reporting and computational-cost disclosure are useful improvements. However, v2 introduces a substantive error in its new central theory: Theorem 5 claims mutual information can be nonmonotonic when variables are appended, although each increment equals a nonnegative conditional mutual information. For the same target, this also contradicts Theorem 6's nonmonotonicity claim for Equation 12's bounds. These statements underpin the expanded scaling argument, substantially weakening scientific reliability relative to v1 and outweighing the reporting improvements.
